A wife's torn-out hair is restored by prayer

The collection tells of a woman in the Limousin, the region where Saint Anthony was then serving. She was very devoted to the friars. She sometimes bought what they needed. Her husband was jealous and had no devotion. One evening she stayed out late on the friars' business and came home at night. Her husband said angrily, “You are coming from your lovers now.” She answered, “It is true that I stayed late for the Friars Minor, whom I love for God's sake.” He was full of rage and seized her by the hair. He dragged her back and forth until he tore out all her hair.

She had all the torn hair gathered up. Enlightened by faith, she laid it on her pillow, arranged it there, and bent her head over it. In the morning she sent for Saint Anthony to come quickly, because she was not well. He thought she wanted to make her confession and hurried to her. She said, “Brother Anthony, see how much I have suffered for your friars.” She told him what had happened and added, “If you will pray to God for me, I know that God will give me back my hair as it was.” Saint Anthony said, “Go, woman. Did you make me come here for this?”

Then he left and called the friars. He told them what had happened to her and what she asked. He said, “Let us pray, brothers. I hope that God will look on her faith.” While Saint Anthony prayed, her hair was set back on her head as it had been. When her husband came home, she showed him her head and told him what had happened. He was amazed and touched inwardly by God. His jealousy left him completely. From then on he served the friars gladly and devotedly.

Saint Anthony foretells a son's martyrdom

The collection tells that Saint Anthony once visited a pregnant lady of Anicium. She asked him to pray for her and her child. He prayed and came back to her. He said, “Stay in good hope and joy. The Lord will give you a son who will be great in the Church of God. He will be a Friar Minor and a martyr, and by his preaching he will lead many to the palm of martyrdom.” She bore a son and named him Philip. He entered the Order of Friars Minor and crossed the sea.

The castle of Azotus was betrayed to the Saracens, and about two thousand Christians were put in the hands of the barbarians. All were condemned to death. Philip was among them. He won the right to be killed last, so that he could strengthen the others. They were asked whether they wanted to deny their faith and escape death. All answered that they would follow the way that Brother Philip chose. He preached to them and told them what the Lord had revealed to him that night: he would enter the glory of heaven by martyrdom with a thousand souls. Then he heard their confessions, and they chose death for the faith of Christ.

They were beheaded one by one while Brother Philip kept preaching. The Sultan was angry and had the joints of Philip's hands cut off piece by piece. Philip did not stop preaching. The Sultan had him skinned up to the navel, but Philip still comforted the Christians. Then the Sultan had his tongue cut out. Even without a tongue he kept preaching with burning zeal until all the others had died by the sword. Last of all he took off his hood with great devotion and was beheaded. He won the palm of martyrdom. The bodies lay unburied for four days. The Sultan came to the place and found them whole and without any stench. He was amazed. Those who did not go back died in peace in the Lord. Saint Anthony told the old man to visit the tombs of the Apostles twelve times. Stories told of Saint Anthony in later centuries

Stories told by Surius and Wadding

Laurentius Surius and Luke Wadding told these stories in the 1500s and 1600s. The Bollandists print them in a supplement to the early Life:

  • a murdered boy at Lisbon is raised from the dead to clear Saint Anthony's father of a charge
  • Saint Anthony appears in a Lisbon court and clears his father over royal money
  • the bones of a capon he ate turn into fish bones
  • a roast owl set before him by heretics tastes like capon
  • Saint Anthony preaches in Italian with perfect ease though he was born far away
  • Saint Anthony appears at night to sleepers and tells them to confess sins that only God knew

The collection of about 1367 tells the last story at more length. It says Saint Anthony was eager for the salvation of souls and used every remedy he could to turn sinners from sin. He appeared at night to many sleeping people and called each by name. They told the friars that he said, “Get up. Go to such a brother or such a priest and confess such a sin, which you committed at such a time in such a place.” Only God had known that sin. In this way many sins that people were too ashamed to confess were wiped away by confession in the sacrament.

Status: told by Surius and Wadding and printed by the Bollandists in a supplement to the early Life. Its last story is also told in the collection of about 1367.

Saint Anthony foretells a notary's martyrdom

Surius and Wadding tell that Saint Anthony was guardian of the friars at Le Puy in France. A notary there lived a worldly life. Whenever Saint Anthony met him he knelt before him with bare head. Saint Beatrice de Silva is freed from prison

The 1883 chronicle tells of Saint Beatrice de Silva. She was a maid of honor to Elizabeth, a princess of Portugal. Elizabeth married John II of Castile in 1441. Saint Beatrice was very beautiful, and the Queen suspected that the King loved her. Saint Beatrice was put in prison and almost starved. She vowed perpetual virginity to Our Lady and was set free in three days. She fled toward Toledo. On the way she met two friars. At first she thought they had been sent to tell her to prepare for death. One of them was Saint Anthony. He told her that she would live and become a mother to many religious virgins. She became a Dominican nun. Many years later she founded a new congregation named for the Immaculate Conception.

The Acta Sanctorum gives more of the story from Wadding and Garibay. Saint Beatrice was a kinswoman of Queen Elizabeth and the dearest of her ladies. She was the sister of James, first Count of Portalegre, and of Blessed Amadeus the Franciscan. Many men fell in love with her beauty. The King liked her more than the Queen wished. The Queen was so hurt that she shut the young woman in a narrow chest and punished her with hunger and thirst. Saint Beatrice prayed in the darkness like Jonah in the whale. She vowed her chastity to God under the protection of the Mother of God if she were rescued from this danger.

The next night the Blessed Virgin appeared to her in a white robe and a blue cloak. The Virgin promised her freedom and kept that promise after three days. Saint Beatrice then fled from the town of Tordesillas to Toledo. Two Franciscans met her unexpectedly. They spoke to her in Portuguese and strengthened her in her purpose. They told her that she would be the mother of many virgins. A little later they vanished from her sight. Afterward Saint Beatrice judged that one of them was Saint Anthony, from the way he spoke and from his signs.

Status: told in the 1883 chronicle, which follows the Portuguese writer Azevedo of the 1700s. The Acta Sanctorum also tells it from Wadding and Garibay.

A precious ring slipped from his finger and fell in. The well was deep and held much water, so he had no hope of getting it back. He was troubled by the sudden loss. Yet he was content to commend the matter to Saint Anthony, and he put aside all further worry.

On the feast day he was praying in Saint Anthony's church as he did every year. His servant came and began to cry out, “Good news, good news! My master's ring has appeared!” The servant told what had happened. While he was drawing water, the bucket fell from his hands into the well. He let down a hook to bring it up. He pulled up the bucket and his master's ring with it. The ring lay at the bottom of the bucket as neatly as if a hand had set it there. Everyone who heard it was moved to thank the Saint aloud.

A lost purse of coins is netted at Setúbal

The Bollandists quote the same recent collection. It tells of a merchant sailing on the river that leads to Setúbal. The Latin text calls the town Cetobriga and says it is commonly written Zetubal. Standing by the mast of the boat, the merchant took out a purse full of coins. The purse was shaken from his hands. It slipped out by way of the sail and fell into the water. While they were singing it, some fishermen let down their net in the same place. Among other things they drew up the purse. It went back to its owner without the loss of a single coin.

Status: told in the Analecta of the Acta Sanctorum, from a recent collection of Saint Anthony's favors.

Two lost rings are found in fish

The Bollandists tell of two rings found in fish after prayer to Saint Anthony:

  • Gonzaga tells of the Franciscan convent at Avilés, which was founded about 1380. A merchant named John Alphonsus and his wife Aldonza Gonzalez honored an image of Saint Anthony there. They asked that all things go well for them through his merits. Each year on his feast day they gave the friars a rich meal. They left houses and lands to their heirs on the condition that the heirs do the same. Their grandson Nicholas Alfonsi lost a ring at sea. The ring had come to him from his parents. As the feast drew near, he sent fishermen to catch fish for the friars' meal. The cook found the lost ring in the stomach of one fish. Everyone credited it to Saint Anthony, and Nicholas most of all. He had the story painted around the statue just as it happened.
  • Pacieco tells of a knight whose ring fell into the water while he showed it to friends. Divers could not find it. The knight was sad. He went to a friend who led the Franciscan convent as its guardian. The guardian saw his sadness and learned the cause. He urged the knight to turn to Saint Anthony and have the friars say one Mass. The knight did so and heard the Mass. Afterward he went to the market and bought fish of different kinds and sizes to send the friars as alms. When one of the fish was cut open, the ring was found inside. The news filled everyone with joy and made the knight more devoted to the Saint.

Status: told by Gonzaga and by Pacieco, whom the Bollandists quote in the Analecta. Gonzaga says the Avilés account is very true and confirmed by trustworthy witnesses.

A bishop's lost ring falls on his table

The Bollandists quote Pacieco on Iñigo Manrique, Bishop of Córdoba and Inquisitor General of Spain. The bishop had a special devotion to Saint Anthony because of the many favors he had received. He lost the ring with which he had been consecrated bishop. He had Masses said for its return. At last he gave up hope of recovering it, and he was very sad about the loss. A few days later he sat at table with many guests. They were speaking of the miracles of the saints. He said that he was very devoted to Saint Anthony and was bound to him for the favors he had received. Then he said, “Now I have something to complain of. He has not revealed to me the thing I hold dear.” He had barely said it when the ring was seen to fall on the table. An unseen hand had thrown it. The bishop and all his guests were filled with wonder, and their devotion to the Saint grew.

An ant carries back a lost bead

The Bollandists tell of a Capuchin lay brother in Sicily. Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscans. The brother had lost a bead from his rosary. He valued it highly because indulgences were attached to it. It had fallen from the rosary without his noticing. He searched for it a long time and gave it up as lost. Then he remembered the antiphon “If you seek miracles.” He said it. At once an ant came straight to him with the bead in its mouth. The brother took it back and shed tears of thanks to the Saint.

The Bollandists add that a famous astrologer named Cortesius knew of such cases. When people asked him to cast a chart to find lost things, he answered, “Gentlemen, my best and truest chart is to call on Saint Anthony. I have tried it many times. Use this method. All the others hold much that is empty and little that is true. They blame innocent people and breed suspicions that have no ground.” In his own writings he printed the antiphon with the Church's prayer for Saint Anthony in the place where he gave the rules for such a chart.

A lost bucket and a lost bond, Antwerp

The Bollandists tell two more stories of lost things:

  • Pacieco tells of a lay friar who was drawing water when the bucket slipped from his hands into the well. He tried many ways to get it back, and he needed the water badly. He ran to the altar of a nearby little chapel and took the wooden statue of Saint Anthony. Then he tied it to a rope and dropped it into the well. He pulled it up again. It turned out just as he had simply and boldly expected. He drew up the bucket together with the statue, because the bucket had caught on the statue's arm.
  • A Bollandist writer tells of something that happened at Antwerp about fifty years before, when he was a boy. A merchant woman of middle fortune had sold goods to a leading merchant woman and received a bond. When payment was due, she could not find the bond. She went to the other woman anyway, because they had traded in good faith for many years. She trusted that she would be believed, and she asked to be believed. Instead she was insulted, as if she were asking to be paid twice. She knew she was honest, and she was stung more by the insult than by the loss of money. She went to a woman known for revealing hidden things. But she met a better adviser, the writer himself. He told her to have a Mass said that same hour in honor of Saint Anthony. She went and heard the Mass. Afterward the other woman's servant told her to stop worrying. His mistress was ready to pay the debt on the first woman's word alone.

A lost boy is found in Japan, 1600

The Bollandists quote Solier's history of the Church in Japan for a story from 1600. It happened in the region of Nagasaki, Arima, and Omura. A boy of three was lost. His parents searched everywhere in vain. They did not know what else to do. They asked one of the Jesuit fathers whether anything more could be done. He told them to make their confession first. Then they were to commend the little boy to the Mother of God, to his guardian angel, and to Saint Anthony, the patron of lost things.

It was a Saturday, so the Jesuit said the Mass of Our Lady for the same intention. He asked all the religious of the house to pray for the case. The boy was found under a very dense thicket toward noon the same day. The account says no one but the devil could have carried him there. He was found completely unharmed. His parents rightly gave the credit to the prayers made for him. The Bollandist writer adds that Jean Bolland had marked this story long before in his notes for 13 June.

A shipwrecked man is saved on the rocks, Algarve

The Bollandists quote Gonzaga for a story about the Franciscan convent founded about 1504 in the Algarve region of Portugal. A man was traveling in a small boat on a stormy sea. He expected nothing but shipwreck. At last the waves threw him against rocks, and he clung to very high cliffs. From the depths of his heart he commended himself to the glorious Virgin Mary and to Saint Anthony of Padua. Through their favor he was rescued from this great danger.

When the people of his country heard of it, they began to build a hermitage above the rocks. Their first fervor cooled, and they did not finish it. Franciscan friars from Castile came to the kingdom and heard of it. In their sermons they urged the neighbors to finish what they had begun. Their words moved the people to build a convent. A noble man named George Hurtado was very devoted to the Franciscans. He gave the first funds from his own means. His example stirred the rest of the people to complete the work.

A man left for dead is raised, Naples 1675

The Bollandists tell of Antonio Tortamano of Montemurro in the kingdom of Naples. He was very devoted to Saint Anthony. In April 1675 he went to Ferrandina to buy linen. On the evening before, he ate supper at a friend's house with two other guests. They had learned from his words that he carried money, or they had guessed it from his errand. Next morning he went down into a valley near Picerno and Baragiano. There the same three men met him. He had dined with them as friends, and now they were robbers. They told him to stand still and tied him up. He called on Saint Anthony twice. At the same moment one of them struck him on the head with a small axe. The man said, “Go on, call on Saint Anthony now.” Then the other two attacked him and stabbed him many times. The first man struck his head eighteen times in all.

They carried him to a ditch and buried him under stones and branches. He lay there for five whole days. His body had begun to decay, and worms had begun to crawl on it. Then the Saint he had called on came. He called the dead man twice by name, as if waking him from sleep. Then he wiped away the blood and took away the worms. Taking him by the hand, he set him on the road that led to Picerno. He left him with these words: “I called you twice because you called me twice. Go now, and do not think of taking revenge or of accusing the men who hurt you. Every day in my honor, say the Our Father and the Hail Mary three times.” Tortamano was almost out of his mind with horror and wonder. He found his strength again and went home.

For two months he said nothing. His household did not dare to cut his hair, because they could see worms moving under it. On the feast of Saint Anthony he spoke his first words: “O Saint Anthony!” Then he told what had happened to him. The whole event happened on 15 April, as a tablet hanging at the altar of the royal church of the Conventual Friars at Naples shows. There the friars keep the signed account. The Bishop of Sant'Angelo and Bisaccia examined Tortamano formally and signed the record. According to the record, Tortamano declared that God had worked an unusual miracle in him. Tortamano later became a friar himself.

Status: told in an account printed at Florence in 1678, as quoted by the Bollandists in the Analecta. The Bollandists add that the signed record is kept at Naples.

A prince is struck on the cheek and converted

The Bollandists quote a letter that Father Vincent Dammey of the Society of Jesus wrote to Rome from Cape Comorin in 1680. A cleric from Bengal had passed through on his way to take holy orders. He said he was hurrying to a very heroic mission. In those parts there was a prince of a pagan nation. He is now named Antonio d'Orufano. The Portuguese had captured him in war about twenty years before. For a long time he held to his own beliefs and would not change. The strongest arguments from others and from the Jesuit fathers did not move him to accept the faith.

At last he was moved by a saving dream or vision. Saint Anthony of Padua appeared to him. Like a loving father, the Saint struck him a hard blow on the cheek. The prince still carries the mark of it on his face. Saint Anthony persuaded him to give up his stubbornness and give his hand to the true faith. He also persuaded him to work for the conversion of his people. The prince did this at once. He asked to be washed in baptism and to be called Anthony. He wanted his mission to carry the same name, and it is commonly called the Mission of Lord Anthony. The writer says this new apostle gave himself and all he owned to the conversion of his people. He taught them by his words and his example, with great fervor and with fruit to match.

A young Indian converts after a vision

The Catholic Encyclopedia says that right after Saint Anthony died, he appeared at Vercelli to Abbot Thomas Gallo. The collection of about 1367 tells it in more detail. It says the Abbot of Vercelli was alone in his room, deep in thought about God, on the day Saint Anthony died. The Abbot thought Saint Anthony was going to his native Spain. He got up and looked for him outside, hoping to keep him a little longer. He asked the monastery servants where Brother Anthony was. They said he had not come. The Abbot insisted that he had just seen him and that Saint Anthony had healed him by a miracle. A message was sent to the friars in the nearby village, but he was not there. Then the Abbot understood that Saint Anthony had gone through death to the feast of heaven. He noted the time. A murder plot against a priest is stopped

The early Latin Life tells of men of Padua who plotted to kill a priest. They set an ambush for him in a certain place. Saint Anthony appeared there in the likeness of a friar they did not know. He would not leave the spot while they waited for the priest. They ordered him to go. He said he knew their intention. They thought someone had betrayed them and asked who he was. He told them he was Saint Anthony. They were stunned and gave up their plan. He led them to confess in public what had happened, and they gave glory to God.

The collection of about 1367 gives the words they spoke. Saint Anthony asked them, “Why are you here? Go away quickly.” They answered, “You, good brother, go your own way, for we will not leave this place.” He said, “I will not leave either.” They asked, “Who are you to give us orders?” He answered, “I am Saint Anthony.” At once they fell to the ground in fear, and he vanished. They went with great gentleness to the priest they had meant to kill. They told him about the vision, and they made peace with him. The whole city heard of it.

Status: told in the early Latin Life among other miracles that it says were no less true than the approved ones though not so solemnly approved. It gives no date. The collection of about 1367 gives the words they spoke.

An arm is healed and then lost again

The early Latin Life tells of a man whose one arm was quite useless. Through Saint Anthony he received full health in it. Then he tried to turn the Lord's gift to a wrong use. He said he would still take revenge on his enemies. At once he lost his strength and fell back into his old weakness.

Status: told in the early Latin Life among other miracles that it says were no less true than the approved ones though not so solemnly approved. It gives no place or date. The collection of about 1367 tells a similar story of a knight.

Tuesday becomes Saint Anthony's day of cures

The 1883 chronicle says that Saint Anthony's body entered Padua on a Tuesday. It says that no sufferer who asked for his help on that day failed to be cured. From this came the custom of honoring him on Tuesdays and on nine Tuesdays in a row.

Some people at the Pope's court objected that a year had not yet passed since Saint Anthony's death. The early Latin Life says God's loving providence sent help. One of the objectors dreamed that Pope Gregory IX was consecrating a church. The Pope asked for saints' remains to place in the altar, but none could be found. A newly dead body lay covered to one side. The Pope had it uncovered. The relics of that body were so precious that everyone present fought to take some. When the man woke, he found the envoys from Padua at his door.

Status: told in the early Latin Life and in Rigauld's Life. Rigauld names the man as a cardinal. The 1883 chronicle adds that the body was whole and sweet-smelling. It says the cardinal met the envoys and said, “This is our dream, and this is what it means.”

Lisbon's bells ring by themselves, 30 May 1232

The 1883 chronicle says that on 30 May 1232 Pope Gregory IX declared Saint Anthony a saint at Spoleto. At that moment all the church bells of Lisbon began to ring by themselves.

The collection of about 1367 tells what the people of Lisbon did that day. Lisbon was Saint Anthony's native city. All its people were celebrating with great joy, and they did not know why. They had heard nothing of the canonization. The bells of the city rang with no one touching them. In this way they told the citizens of Saint Anthony's glory. A short time later the people learned that Saint Anthony had been made a saint that very day. Lisbon then dedicated the high altar of its cathedral to him. It keeps his feast there each year with a solemn celebration.

Status: told in the 1883 chronicle, which says writers of that time tell it. The collection of about 1367 tells what the people of Lisbon did that day.

Miracles at Saint Anthony's old bed in Coimbra

Rigauld writes that the bed Saint Anthony slept in at the Holy Cross monastery at Coimbra became an object of great honor. He says that people who ask Saint Anthony's help there receive many miracles.

Status: told in Rigauld's Life, at second hand. Rigauld says the Custodian of St. Jacques told him about the bed. A Custodian was a friar who led a group of friaries.

Saint Anthony announces a queen's death at Coimbra

Rigauld writes that after Saint Anthony was canonized, the Queen of Portugal died in a distant part of her kingdom. Saint Anthony appeared to one of the canons of the Holy Cross monastery at Coimbra, where he had lived as a young man. He spoke kindly to the canon and told him of the Queen's death almost at the hour it happened. Rigauld says the news helped the community and freed it from many worries.

Status: told in Rigauld's Life.

Saint Anthony's drowned nephew lives again

The 1883 chronicle says Saint Anthony's sister had a son at Lisbon named Apparizio. He went out in a boat with other boys. A gust of wind overturned it, and he drowned. His mother kept the body for three days and would not allow it to be buried. She prayed to her brother and promised her son to him if he would win back the boy's life. The chronicle says the boy came back to life as soon as she made the vow. Later he kept her promise by entering the Franciscan Order.

The collection of about 1367 gives the mother's prayer. It names the boy Parisius and says he was about five years old. He was playing in the sea with other boys when their little boat tipped over. He alone sank, while the others swam. After three hours his mother ran there and took his dead body from the fishermen. His father wanted to bury him. His mother cried out, “Either leave him with me, or bury me with him.” Then she turned to Saint Anthony and said in tears, “My brother, you are wonderful and kind to strangers. Will you be cruel to your sister? Have mercy on me, a wretched woman, and give me back my son. I promise to give him to God's service in your Order.” The boy rose up unharmed. His mother kept her vow, and he lived and died in the Order.

Status: told in the 1883 chronicle and by the Basilica of Saint Anthony. Some sources spell the boy's name Parrisio. The collection of about 1367 gives the mother's prayer.

The Basilica of Saint Anthony tells of a girl of Padua named Eurilia. She went with her mother to visit an old woman and stayed outside to gather sticks. Her mother begged Saint Anthony to give her daughter back. Soon Eurilia's lips began to twitch. She coughed up the water and grew warm again.

A drowned baby lives again, Padua

Rigauld tells of an infant named Thomazino whose parents lived close to the church of Saint Anthony. His mother left him near a vessel of water. He saw his reflection and tried to catch it. He fell in head first and drowned. His mother found him cold and stiff and cried out so loudly that the neighborhood gathered. A friar and some workmen from the church went away sorrowful. She begged Saint Anthony to raise her son and promised that she would give the poor as much corn as her child weighed. From evening until midnight the child lay dead, and the mother kept calling on the saint and renewing her vow. Then he came to life in perfect health.

Status: told in Rigauld's Life about 1300 as one of the miracles Brother Peter Raymund recorded at Padua in 1293. The Basilica of Saint Anthony tells it of a twenty-month-old boy named Tommy who fell into a pot of boiling water. In that telling the mother promises bread for the poor. A voice from the tomb promises Padua's freedom

In 1237 the tyrant Ezzelino da Romano took Padua. The 1883 chronicle says that one night a friar named Bartolomeo Corradini was praying at Saint Anthony's tomb. He heard a voice from the tomb say, “I promise you that a week after my feast this city will be freed from its oppressor.” On Tuesday 20 June the armies of the Pope and of Venice beat Ezzelino's nephew Ansidisio at the gates of Padua.

The collection of about 1367 says that Brother Bartholomew Corradini was the guardian of the friars of Padua. The Church's legate and his army had surrounded the city. On the night of Saint Anthony's feast Brother Bartholomew kept vigil at the tomb. He begged with tears for the city's freedom. A clear voice sounded from the tomb: “Brother Bartholomew, do not be afraid, and do not be so sad. On the octave of my feast the city of Padua will be freed. It will enjoy its old liberty and freedom again.” The octave is the eighth day of a feast, one week after the feast day. Several friars who were keeping vigil in the church said that they had really heard the voice. When the people of Padua learned of it, they decided to keep that octave every year with great joy. The collection says they still keep it.

Status: told in the 1883 chronicle, which names Pope Alexander IV but no year. The Basilica of Saint Anthony tells that Saint Anthony appeared to two friars, one perhaps Blessed Luke Belludi, and foretold the freeing of Padua. It gives the year 1256. The collection of about 1367 tells it too.

Saint Anthony's tongue is found fresh, 1263

In 1263 the friars moved Saint Anthony's body to the new church at Padua. Saint Bonaventure led the move as head of the Franciscan Order. In the tomb the flesh had turned to dust. The tongue was fresh and bright red. Saint Bonaventure kissed it and said, “Blessed tongue, you always blessed the Lord and made others bless him. Now it is plain how highly God valued you.” Rigauld says he showed the tongue with great joy to everyone present.

Status: told by Rigauld about 1300, by the 1883 chronicle, and by the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1913. A friar's hernia closes at the tomb

Rigauld tells of a friar named Cambius from Romagna. He suffered so badly from a hernia that no doctor or steel support could help him. He came to Padua shortly before the feast of Saint Anthony. On the feast he saw the sick healed at the tomb and began to hope for his own cure. A dense crowd kept him from the tomb. Cambius stretched out his right hand and touched it. He laid the hand on his body and felt relief. Then he touched the tomb again and laid his hand on the place of the hernia. The wound closed and became as hard as his forehead. He leaped and danced. “A short time ago I could not have done that,” he said. “Now I can leap and dance, thanks to the help of Blessed Anthony!” Full of gratitude, he joined the friars of that province to serve Saint Anthony.

A growth on a lady's head is healed

Rigauld tells of a lady of the diocese of Forlì. For ten years she had had a harmful growth the size of a fist on her skull. No doctor could help her. She vowed to circle Saint Anthony's tomb with a silver chain if he healed her. That night she dreamed that Saint Anthony cut the growth in four parts without pain. Soon after, the growth opened into four parts as in the dream. It gave off much matter. Her head was left sound and without a mark. She went to Padua proclaiming the praises of Saint Anthony, and she kept her vow and put the silver chain around the tomb.

The collection of about 1367 names the lady Beatrix. It says she vowed to go around Saint Anthony's altar with a silver thread if he gave her back her health. That night Saint Anthony appeared to her and divided the growth into four parts. She kept her vow and went to Padua. There she put the silver thread around his tomb.

Status: told in Rigauld's Life from Brother Peter Raymund's collection of 1293. The collection of about 1367 names her Beatrix.

A mute friar speaks again at the tomb

Rigauld tells of Bernardin, a friar of Parma who had lost his voice for two months. He was so weak that he could not blow out a candle held close to his mouth. Doctors had burned his throat nine times with a hot iron. He wrote to the head of his province for leave to go to Padua. There he prayed at the tomb and began to cough. He brought up a quantity of matter. His health and his speech came back at once. He broke out in praise of the saint and began the Salve Regina in a loud voice. The Salve Regina is the Church's hymn to the Blessed Virgin Mary. The friars joined him with joy, and he sang in thanksgiving for the miracle done before everyone's eyes.

A deaf and mute servant hears and speaks

Rigauld tells of a servant in a convent of nuns at Padua. He was twenty-five and had been born deaf and mute. His tongue was very short and twisted. He could not hear bells rung close to his ears. Ladies of the city and his companions swore to this before the Bishop of Padua. Three times he was told in a vision to seek Saint Anthony. He prayed in the church all day and all night. About the ninth hour a bright light shone around him. His tongue grew to its proper size. He cried out, “Blessed be our Lord Jesus Christ and Blessed Antony!” He then spoke whole sentences clearly though he had never learned language. Rigauld says God himself gave him the words. The nuns he served praised the saint who had opened his ears and loosed his tongue. His name was Peter, and the crowds urged him to take the name Antony.

A man's lost eyes and tongue are restored

Rigauld tells of a man near Padua who wanted to learn secret things by calling up spirits. One night he sat in a magic circle with a clerk who knew the spells. Demons appeared with terrible howling. The man was too afraid to answer them. They tore out his tongue and his eyes. He lived on in that state and could not even confess his sin. He remembered the wonders God worked through Saint Anthony and had himself taken to the church. At the Mass the priest raised the Sacred Host, and at that moment God gave him back his eyes. The crowd begged God to give him back his tongue too. His tongue was restored while the choir sang the Agnus Dei. The Agnus Dei is a chant of the Mass. He cried out that God had given him back his sight and speech through Saint Anthony.

A note from Saint Anthony frees a woman

Rigauld tells of a woman in Portugal who was often troubled by a devil. Her husband once said in anger that she was possessed. She went out to drown herself. On the way she passed the friars' church on the feast of Saint Anthony. She went in to commend herself to God before she died. She fell asleep and saw Saint Anthony in a vision. He told her to keep a note that would protect her from the devil. She woke with a piece of parchment in her hand. It said, “Look, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has won the right to open the book and break its seals.” She was no longer troubled while she kept it. The king asked to see it and would not give it back. The devil troubled her again until her husband got a copy from the friars. That copy protected her as well.

The collection of about 1367 tells it at Santarém in the time of King Dionysius. It says the woman was a sinner with great devotion to Saint Anthony. The devil tormented her and tempted her to kill herself. It seemed to her that Christ spoke in her heart. He said she had done so much wrong against him that she could not be saved unless she killed herself. Then the devil appeared to her and said, “I am the one you have offended. If you go to the river Tagus and drown yourself there to pay for your faults, I will forgive all your sins and give you eternal glory.” Her husband was away, and the devil kept urging her. One day she was deceived and went toward the Tagus.

She passed the friars' church on the feast of Saint Anthony and went in to commend herself to him. There she fell on her face before the altar in the chapel of Saint Anthony and prayed in tears. She asked him to show her whether God wanted her to drown herself or to give up that plan altogether. As she prayed, she fell gently asleep. Saint Anthony appeared to her and told her to keep a note that would free her from the devil. She woke and found on her neck a piece of parchment with golden letters. It said, “Look at the Cross of the Lord; flee, you hostile powers; the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered; alleluia, alleluia.” At once the temptation left her. While she kept the note, the devil did not trouble her.

King Dionysius heard of it from her husband and took the note. At once the devil attacked her again. Her husband could not get the note back. With the help of the friars he got a copy from the King and gave it to her. The copy freed her as the first note had. She confessed with tears and turned wholly to God. She lived a godly life for twenty years and ended her days in peace. King Dionysius put the note among his relics. Many wonders were done when people called on Saint Anthony with it.

Status: told in Rigauld's Life. Rigauld says Brother Peter Raymund assured him that it was true. The collection of about 1367 tells it at Santarém in the time of King Dionysius.

Dry vines bear grapes and fill a mocker's cup

The collection tells that some people were speaking together about the miracles of the saints. One of them praised Saint Anthony's wonders. Among them he told of the glass that did not break when an unbeliever threw it from a height onto stones. Another man laughed at this. He took an empty glass cup and held dry vines in his hand. He said, “If Saint Anthony made grapes grow from these vines and filled this cup with fresh juice, I would count that a miracle. Then I would believe the miracle you told us about the cup.”

At once the vines turned green and were covered with leaves. Then grapes grew on them, flowered, and ripened. Wine was pressed from the grapes, and the glass cup was filled completely. The people were amazed. The mockers became praisers.

The collection tells that Saint Anthony shone at Padua with many miracles. Some heretics laughed at his wonders. They wanted to announce in public that the miracles were false, so they came to Padua. They said that he had been blinded unjustly and asked all the people to beg Saint Anthony for his sight. An hour passed like this. Then the man who had pretended to be blind cried out, “Blessed Anthony has given me back my sight!”

His companions ran up and pulled off the cloth, so that they could mock the false miracle before the people. But both of his eyes stayed on the cloth, and the tricksters were tricked. They were terrified and moved in their hearts. They confessed the fraud in public. After a devout prayer they all received the light of faith. Through Saint Anthony the man also received the light of his eyes.

Then he was cleansed and healed of his leprosy.

The collection tells of an abbot who felt pity for a faithful servant. The man had been mute and deaf for twenty years, so the abbot made a vow to Saint Anthony. If Saint Anthony would restore the servant to health, the abbot would give him to Saint Anthony forever to guard his altar. The abbot sent the man to Saint Anthony's tomb. A dying princess of Portugal is healed

The collection tells of Lady Aldonsa. She was the daughter of Taraxia, Queen of Portugal. She was so ill that the doctors gave her up, and no hope for her life remained. Her mother the Queen was crushed with grief. She turned to Saint Anthony with many tears and called on his help devoutly: “Help me, most holy Father, for you were born in this kingdom. Pray to the Lord to give my daughter health.”

About midnight the girl Aldonsa slept a little. She saw Saint Anthony. He said to her, “Do you know me? I am Saint Anthony. I have come to you because your mother's prayers called me. So choose one of two things. You may pay the debt of the flesh. Then the Lord will forgive your sins and the punishment due for them, and today you will be with me in paradise. Or you may stay in the world with your mother, and I will give you back your health at once.” She loved bodily health more, and she was healed then and there. In the vision she took hold of the cord that Saint Anthony wore. She began to cry out and call her mother, “Lady, here is Blessed Anthony, who has made me well!” The Queen ran in with other ladies and found her daughter well. They all gave thanks to God and Saint Anthony.

Saint Francis and Saint Anthony reach a dying lady

The collection tells of a powerful lady named Lupa at Linhares in Portugal. She was devoted to Saint Francis and Saint Anthony. A demon had served her in the form of a woman as her chambermaid, and she had lived in cruelty and many crimes. In her last illness she lost hope because of the greatness of her sins. She did not care for her soul and would not make her confession, though people urged her. She lay there sad and without hope. Two Friars Minor came in. They comforted her and urged her to confess and repent. She refused. She said she had committed so many sins that God would not show mercy for any penance of hers.

The friar who looked older said, “Confess and be sorry. I take your penance on myself, and I give you a share in my goods. By the power of the Lord's Passion I promise you eternal life.” At these words the lady changed for the better and was given courage to repent. She turned from a wolf into a lamb. She was sorry for her sins and confessed with many tears. Then she asked for the robe of the Friars Minor and received it from that friar's hand. She fell asleep in the Lord and died happy. At once the friars vanished. Everyone thought it reasonable that they were Saint Francis and Saint Anthony, to whom she was so devoted and whom she always called to her aid. She was buried in the convent at Guarda.

Later a squire wanted to go to Linhares, where the lady had died. One night he heard a voice like a woman's. It cried, “O wretched me! For thirteen years I served badly, and I labored in vain.” The squire was terrified. He made the sign of the cross and said, “I command you by Jesus Christ, say who you are.” The voice answered, “I am the devil. For thirteen years I served Lady Lupa in the form of a woman and helped her in many crimes. I wanted to take her to the depths of hell after her death. But at the end two Friars Minor in hoods came, whom she had loved before. They turned her toward repentance. They snatched her soul out of my power and took her with them to the joys of heaven.”

The devil gave him a sign that this was true. When the squire came to Linhares, he would hear that a smith had killed his wife and would be hanged for it. The devil said he had caused that killing and would lead the souls of the smith and his wife to hell. The squire went to Linhares and found the smith already hanged for killing his wife. He told what he had heard, to everyone's amazement.

Status: told in the collection of his miracles written about 1367.

Source: Liber miraculorum (about 1367), printed in Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), nn. 51–52, p. 227, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

Saint Francis and Saint Anthony save a woman

The collection tells of a woman named Seri in a castle in Portugal. She had a special devotion to Saint Francis and Saint Anthony. Her husband was a wicked man. He had left her and lived with other women. He hated her and often beat her and hurt her in many ways. Her sorrow grew until she lost all hope. She decided to end her troubles by hanging herself. One night her husband was away, and the household was asleep. She set up a rope in the room and was about to put her neck in the noose, as the devil urged her. Someone knocked loudly at the door and cried out. She hid the rope and went to see who it was.

She opened the door and saw two Friars Minor. They humbly asked her to take them in for the love of God. She asked where they came from and what their names were. They answered, “We come from far away. One of us is called Francis, and the other Anthony.” She said, “Come in, for love of Saint Francis and Saint Anthony.” She set a table for them, and they gave her new strength with sacred words. Out of respect for them she decided not to do that night what the enemy of mankind had urged. The friars went into the room that was given them for sleeping, and the woman went to bed.

At the same hour the two friars appeared to her husband. They said, “We are Saint Francis and Saint Anthony, sent by God to tell you this. Turn from your evil way. Send away your other women and stay with your wife, who is devoted to us. If you do not, you will die in three days and fall into hell. This night your wife would have hanged herself because of your cruelty, if we had not come to her door. Go to her, and as a sign ask her for the rope she meant to use.” The man woke suddenly, afraid and sorry for his sins. In the morning he got up and went to his house.

His wife had risen too. She did not find the friars. She found the bed made, as if no one had slept in it. This amazed her. All the doors were shut, and she could not think how the friars had gone out. Her husband came in and greeted her kindly. He said, “Dearest, where is the rope you wanted to hang yourself with last night?” She stood astonished. He said, “I know well what a favor they did you. Saint Francis and Saint Anthony have freed you and me from death of body and soul, and you took them in last night.” Then he told his vision and humbly asked his wife's pardon. They lived together for a long time in love and peace. They did many good works and praised Saint Francis and Saint Anthony together.

Status: told in the collection of his miracles written about 1367.

Source: Liber miraculorum (about 1367), printed in Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), nn. 55–56, pp. 227–228, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

A woman rises at her burial with a vision

The collection tells of a married woman in the village of Elbrun, near the castle of Torres Novas in Portugal. On the feast of Saint Anthony she was carrying a sack of wheat on her head to be ground. She was walking with a girl. A violent wind struck her from the front. It threw the sack to the ground and made her fall on her back. At once a young man with a shining face came and took her soul. He led her along a very wide road to a deep pit that was dark and terrible. Terrible flames seemed to rise from its mouth to the sky. Black and foul smoke came out of it. From inside she heard the roars of the tormentors and the tormented, with weeping and great howling.

She looked in, trembling, and saw demons torturing many kinds of people, each for the deeds by which they had sinned. Cheating merchants wore burning purses around their necks. Moneylenders were fed burning coins. Robbers, adulterers, murderers, false witnesses, and judges were tormented with fitting punishments. She asked the young man what the place was, and he said it was the pit of hell. She saw there many people who were still living. They had been given places there and walked with demons. They were from the city of Lisbon and the town of Santarém, and she named them. She had never been to those places. The collection says it should not seem unbelievable that things still to come are shown in such a vision as if they were present.

After this the young man led her to another place, pleasant and full of joy. It was bright with grasses of many kinds and adorned with all kinds of flowers and fruits. She saw a very large and high tent. Bright men came out of it two by two in procession. They wore garments of many kinds and crowns on their heads. At the end came one who was like a bridegroom, dressed in wonderful splendor. The whole procession seemed to be held in his honor. She asked who the place was for and who the people were. The young man said that it was the resting place of souls and that everyone there was saved. He said the bridegroom who came with such splendor was Saint Anthony. His feast was kept in heaven by the saints, far more splendidly than on earth. At the feasts of other saints, others kept the feast in turn. He told her, “You were led here and shown these things so that on the feasts of saints you will stay away from servile work. Give the saints the reverence they are owed, and above all keep away from evil works.”

While her soul was being led, people carried her body to the castle to bury it. She seemed completely dead. The grave was being made ready, and everyone who saw her was amazed and afraid. The woman rose up. She told her whole vision in order, first to the people there, then to many others, and to the writer who set this down.

Status: told in the collection of his miracles written about 1367. The writer says that the woman told him the vision herself.

Source: Liber miraculorum (about 1367), printed in Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), nn. 57–58, p. 228, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

Saint Anthony's statue shakes its head, Bordeaux 1367

The collection tells that in 1367 the Prince of Aquitaine, Edward, gathered a large army. He meant to help King Peter of Castile, whom his illegitimate brother Henry had driven out of his kingdom. The Prince ordered a surgeon named Peter, who lived in the city of Bordeaux, to follow his army and treat the wounded. Peter found this heavy and bitter. He saw that the Prince's will was firm, and he did not dare to resist. Peter had a special devotion to Saint Anthony. He went with confidence to the friars' house at Bordeaux. At his request a friar said a Mass of Saint Anthony in a chapel that held a carved wooden statue of him.

Peter heard the Mass devoutly and looked at the statue. He prayed with great fervor. If the trip was not good for his soul, he asked Saint Anthony to stop it in his mercy. If it was good, he asked him to make Peter willing to go. He saw the statue's head move from side to side as he prayed. It was as if the statue were saying no. Peter was astonished. He thought it might be his own strong imagination. He gathered all his strength and looked again carefully, and he said the prayer again. Again he saw the wooden statue shake its head, as if refusing.

After the Mass he left in wonder. He did not know what the sign meant. Perhaps Saint Anthony was telling him not to go with the army. Or perhaps the sign meant that his going would be good for his soul. He went home confused and unsure. A little later a messenger came from the Prince and told him to come at once. Peter went to the Prince's house, and the Seneschal met him. The Seneschal asked, “Are you ready to go with the Prince to Spain, as he ordered you?” Peter was afraid and answered, “Lord, I am ready to do the Prince's will in everything.” The Seneschal smiled and answered cheerfully, “You speak well, as a good and faithful man. For your comfort the Prince allows you to stay here, unless you receive another order.” Peter went gladly to the friars' church and thanked Saint Anthony. He told the story to some of the friars.

Status: told in the collection of his miracles written about 1367. Peter swore an oath before the friars that it was true.

Source: Liber miraculorum (about 1367), printed in Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), nn. 66–67, p. 230, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

Men sent to destroy his picture are struck down

The collection tells that in the time of Pope Boniface VIII the apse of the Lateran basilica of the Saviour in Rome was being decorated. Two skilled Friars Minor were chosen to make the mosaic. They finished the pictures the Pope had ordered. They saw that there was still room for other pictures. On their own, or perhaps by God's prompting, they painted Saint Francis and Saint Anthony on either side. Out of envy, some clerics told the Pope. The Pope said, “We will put up with the picture of Saint Francis, since it is already there. But what are we to do here with Saint Anthony of Padua? Go and destroy his picture, and have a picture of Saint Gregory made in its place.”

The clerics went up one after another. They later confessed that a terrible figure appeared to them there and threw them down from the height to the floor. They seemed to go mad, and they were stopped from doing what they had planned. The painter friars said that some of them died at once and the others all died within a short time. The Pope heard this. He told those who reported it, “Let that Saint stand as he wishes. As we plainly see, we could sooner perish than gain anything in dealing with him.”

Status: told in the collection of his miracles written about 1367. The collection says the painter friars told it themselves.

Source: Liber miraculorum (about 1367), printed in Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), n. 70, p. 230, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

Saint Francis and Saint Anthony heal a benefactor

The collection tells of a rich and powerful man in Portugal named Peter Peters. He was so attached to the Friars Minor that he gave them a place to build a convent and gave much more for the buildings. One night he was gravely ill. Four friars and many others kept watch in his room and waited for him to die. Out of devotion he kept with him the friars' robe in which he had chosen to be buried. Two Friars Minor appeared to him, one on his right and one on his left. One said, “Peter, do you know us?” He answered, “I know that you are Friars Minor, but I do not know who you are.”

The friar said, “I am Saint Francis, and this is Saint Anthony. You have always been devoted to us, and you have done good to our friars in this convent. So we are sent to comfort you and to cure this illness.” Peter earnestly asked Saint Francis to bless the robe he had with him. After that blessing both friars vanished. Peter recovered so quickly that everyone there was astonished. He lived twelve more years and carried the key to no treasure but the chest that held the blessed robe. He died and was buried in it.

Status: told in the collection of his miracles written about 1367.

Source: Liber miraculorum (about 1367), printed in Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), n. 71, pp. 230–231, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

A lame man of Vicenza is healed, 1346

A Bollandist note in the Acta Sanctorum quotes the Padua chronicle of the Cortusi. It says that in 1346 a man of Vicenza had a broken leg and limped. He often suffered pain, and he could not be freed from it. A dream told him to visit the body of Saint Anthony at Padua with ceremony. He did so and received his health again. The chronicle adds that in the same year many miracles happened through Saint Anthony at Padua. Many sinful women saw them and turned to repentance.

Status: told in the Padua chronicle of the Cortusi, as quoted in a Bollandist note in the Acta Sanctorum.

Source: Note quoting the chronicle of Guilielmus and Albrigetus Cortusius (Novitates Paduae), Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), p. 232 (note), https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

A mocker's weakened hand and arm are healed, 1350

The same chronicle tells that in 1350 the Duke of Poland came to Padua on his way to Rome. The Bollandists note that 1350 was a Jubilee year, when crowds of pilgrims went to Rome. Before he went on, he wanted to visit the shrines of Saint Prosdocimus and Saint Justina. He admired the beauty of the church of Saint Anthony and asked about it. He learned that it was the church of the Father of the city. One of the Duke's companions laughed at the Saint. He said, “Is this really Anthony, in whose name the pigs wear little bells?” At once God's judgment fell on him. His hand and arm went weak. It was the hand he had pointed at the church as he spoke.

The Duke was amazed and asked the cause of the sign. His son told him everything that had happened. The Duke thought about what to do. A light from heaven came to him. He said, “Let us ask with prayers the one who struck him.” He brought the sinner in person before the tomb of Saint Anthony. The man wept and prayed most devotedly. God gave the nobleman back his former health through the prayers of Saint Anthony and for love of him. The Duke was amazed and glad, and the whole city rejoiced with him. Citizens gathered, and the Saint was praised with prayers and offerings. The chronicle says it happened on 10 April of that year.

Status: told in the Padua chronicle of the Cortusi, as quoted in a Bollandist note and in the Analecta of the Acta Sanctorum.

Source: Note quoting the chronicle of Guilielmus and Albrigetus Cortusius (Novitates Paduae), Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), p. 232 (note), https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

Source: Analecta on Saint Anthony of Padua, Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), n. 28, p. 244, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

A cardinal thanks Saint Anthony for his life

In 1350 Saint Anthony's body was moved again at Padua. A cardinal named Guy gave a silver urn for the body and a case for the jaw. The Basilica says Guy de Boulogne had been cured of the plague through Saint Anthony's help. The 1883 chronicle calls him Guy of Montfort. It says his life had been saved through Saint Anthony's prayers, and he came to the shrine on a pilgrimage of thanksgiving.

The Acta Sanctorum says the cardinal was Guy, Bishop of Porto and the Pope's legate in Italy. It says he remembered that he had been freed from death through Saint Anthony's merits and prayers. For that reason he ordered a fine silver case made for the jaw.

Status: told by the Basilica of Saint Anthony and in the 1883 chronicle. The Acta Sanctorum names him as Guy, Bishop of Porto, and tells why he gave the case.

Source: Basilica of St. Anthony, Padua, “Expositions,” https://www.santantonio.org/en/node/578

Source: H. J. Coleridge, ed., The Chronicle of St. Antony of Padua (1883), p. 201, https://archive.org/details/MN5128ucmf_2

Source: Appendix §2, n. 78, Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), p. 234, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

A Jesuit repents before Saint Anthony's tongue relic

The 1883 chronicle tells of a Portuguese Jesuit named Ignatius Martini. A Jesuit is a priest of the Society of Jesus. He was a popular preacher who had grown fond of applause. He visited Padua to honor Saint Anthony's relics. There he kissed the case that holds Saint Anthony's tongue and felt sorrow for the vain use he had made of his own.

The Acta Sanctorum gives the year 1581 for this visit. It says Father Ignatius Martinez was Portuguese. He was going home from the General Congregation of his Society at Rome. He was over sixty years old. At Padua he came to the tabernacle that held the tongue and kissed it out of reverence. He was changed at once, so that he seemed to have taken on the spirit and tongue of Saint Anthony. He gave up the manner of the old orators and began to preach like an apostle. His preaching had so much spirit and fruit that it stirred all Portugal. For the next sixteen years he taught Christian doctrine to children, poor people, soldiers, and prisoners in the galleys.

Status: told in the 1883 chronicle. The Acta Sanctorum gives the year 1581; the 1883 chronicle says the 1600s.

Source: H. J. Coleridge, ed., The Chronicle of St. Antony of Padua (1883), pp. 199–200, https://archive.org/details/MN5128ucmf_2

Source: Appendix §1, n. 77, Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), pp. 233–234, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

Lost things found through Saint Anthony

The 1883 chronicle records things found through Saint Anthony's help in the 1500s and 1600s. They include a manuscript of the theologian Ambrosius Catharinus, a church worker's incense burner, and money that belonged to King Charles II. Catholics ask Saint Anthony especially for help with lost things. The story of Saint Anthony's own stolen book is also tied to this devotion. It is told earlier in this list.

The chronicle tells the first two stories at more length. Ambrosius Catharinus had lost a manuscript. He promised to mention the favor in the book if the Saint helped him get it back. Soon an unknown person came up to him and asked whether he had lost a manuscript. A church worker had lost a valuable incense burner. He told this to the man who had stolen it. The thief proposed that they go together to hear a Mass in honor of Saint Anthony at the friars' church nearby. There they would pray to the Saint to show who had taken it. During the Mass the thief took his handkerchief from his pocket. He had forgotten that a piece of the burner's chain was in the pocket too. The chain fell out, and the thief's prayer was answered to his own shame.

The Acta Sanctorum gives the Catharinus story from his own book on the glory of the saints, printed at Lyon in 1541. He was a Dominican bishop. He set out from Toulouse with a companion and carried a manuscript to take to the printer. It held his notes for debates with heretics. The whole bundle fell from him on the road. He did not notice until he had gone several leagues. Then he went back to Toulouse by the same road and found nothing. Catharinus did all he could and asked his friend the governor of the city to help, but it was in vain. He set out again, sad.

Human help had failed, so he remembered Saint Anthony. He vowed that if he recovered the papers through the Saint's prayers, he would add this favor to the other praises of the saints in his book. He had hardly spoken when a traveler came up to him and asked whether he had lost a book with some papers. Catharinus said yes and described how it could be recognized. The traveler led him to the place where everything lay, with nothing missing. He knew what a favor he had received and told the whole story in his book.

Status: told in the 1883 chronicle. The friars sing the responsory “Si quaeris miracula” in his honor. The Basilica says Julian of Speyer wrote it in 1233. For the first story the Acta Sanctorum draws on Catharinus's own book.

Source: H. J. Coleridge, ed., The Chronicle of St. Antony of Padua (1883), pp. 213–214, https://archive.org/details/MN5128ucmf_2

Source: N. Dal-Gal, “St. Anthony of Padua,” Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Catholic_Encyclopedia_(1913)/St._Anthony_of_Padua

Source: Basilica of St. Anthony, Padua, “Si quaeris miracula,” https://santantonio.org/en/node/583

Source: Analecta on Saint Anthony of Padua, Acta Sanctorum, June, 13 June (1867 reprint), n. 22, p. 242, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum23unse

No one hurt in Padua's fire or storm

The 1883 chronicle says a fire broke out at Padua in 1749. People climbed onto the burning roof. Blazing beams fell on some of them, but no one was hurt. Saint Anthony's altar was not damaged. In a storm in August 1756 the lead roof of the city hall was carried off. The hall was full of people, and no one was injured.

Status: told in the 1883 chronicle.

Source: H. J. Coleridge, ed., The Chronicle of St. Antony of Padua (1883), pp. 202–203, https://archive.org/details/MN5128ucmf_2

A Note on the Sources

The early Latin Life is the one the Bollandists printed; a 1904 editor took it for the Life by Julian of Speyer. Tellers place some stories in different towns. The fish sermon is set at Rimini and near Padua. The kneeling animal is set at Rimini and at Toulouse. The Child Jesus is set at Camposampiero, at Padua, and in the Limousin. The appearance in the friars' choir is set at Limoges and at Montpellier. The humbling of Ezzelino is set at Verona and at Bassano. The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1913 holds that Saint Anthony went to Verona in 1230 to ask Ezzelino to free prisoners. It calls the tyrant's humbling a legend of doubtful origin and says Saint Anthony may have failed. It says the documents do not decide where the Child Jesus appeared. Baring-Gould read the fish in the sermon as a later addition to a story that rebukes men who will not listen. The Catholic Encyclopedia credits the responsory “Si quaeris” to Julian of Speyer, and the 1883 chronicle gives it to Saint Bonaventure. These are the views of modern writers. The Order and the Church have handed the stories down as they are told above. The Bollandist notes in the Acta Sanctorum ask which queen is meant in the accounts of the two princesses, and they would date the surgeon's story to 1366 rather than 1367. This list tells the accounts of the Ancona manuscript and of the collection of about 1367, both printed in the Acta Sanctorum. A few of their accounts are left out because they only repeat another account or give a general statement.

teachings.teachings:
Anthony left no letters and no treatise for ordinary readers. What survives is his Latin sermons: a cycle for the Sundays of the year; an unfinished cycle for the feasts of the saints, which the Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia asked him to write in 1230 and which he worked on at Padua that winter; and sermons for Lent printed in the sixteenth century. They are notes for preachers rather than finished sermons, built from long chains of Bible texts, and his 1911 English biographer warned that they “cannot be judged from their written records.” The sermon passages below are in that biographer’s English (C. M. Antony, 1911). For two passages, the vine and the purple of the poor, our researchers checked the Latin of a 1521 printed edition; the other passages have not yet been checked against the Latin. In 1946 Pope Pius XII named him a Doctor of the Church, the Evangelical Doctor, for the richness of these sermons. Two popular texts are not his: the rhyme “Tony, Tony, turn around,” whose origin is unknown, and the responsory “Si quaeris miracula,” which the Catholic Encyclopedia gives to Julian of Speyer and an 1883 chronicle to Bonaventure.

Sermons in vines, spiders and cranes

Anthony drew his sermons from the world around him: a vine, a spider’s web, a flock of cranes, the lilies of the field. His 1911 biographer pictures him walking the vineyards around Padua, though the sermons themselves do not say where he stood. In a Lenten sermon for the Friday of the second week of Lent, which survives in the old Latin (“Moraliter vinea ista est homo vel anima”), the vine is the soul.

“Man’s soul is a vine, … for to bring forth fruit it must be carefully and ceaselessly cultivated. … The vine left to itself becomes the wildest of all growing things. Its wood is useless, except to burn, when it is dry.”

— Anthony of Padua, Lenten sermon, in C. M. Antony’s English (1911)

Elsewhere the spider becomes the devil, who “spreads his web like a spider” and works inward toward the heart, and the cranes become a picture of a community: one flies in front and calls to the others, and so Christians should “point out by your good example the way of Truth to those that know it not, help on those who are slow, soothe those who are too hasty.” Anthony had spent eight years at Coimbra reading, and the early Lives say his memory served him in place of books; in his sermons that learning goes out into the fields.

The purple of the poor

Anthony preached hard against the ways men grew rich at others’ expense: theft, usury and dishonest gain. Fine clothes bought with such money, he said, were dyed in the blood of the poor. The Latin of this Lenten passage survives in the old printed editions: “O quot induuntur hodie purpura, panno tincto sudore et sanguine pauperis.”

“How many rich men of our day are clad in purple — that is in stuffs dyed with the sweat and blood of the poor, because the clothes they wear are woven out of theft, larceny, usury, and illegitimate gain? … But the garment dyed with the blood of the poor shall be the prey of eternal flames.”

— Anthony of Padua, Lenten sermon, in C. M. Antony’s English (1911)

The usurer, he said, was worse than Judas, who at least brought the thirty pieces back. The remedy was to give: “when the bucket of almsgiving is let down into the well of riches it makes their possession purer to the conscience and more agreeable to God.” He lived this in the pulpit of Padua. In the Lent of 1231, the early Life says, usurers gave back what they had taken, and on 15 March of that year the city passed a law to protect debtors, a copy of which survives in a museum in Padua.

Shepherds who go to law

Anthony spared his own Church nothing. He compared bishops who stayed away from their people to idols, with “hands to gather money, but not to touch the wounds of Christ,” and he asked priests who sued for property where they had learned such things.

“Tell me, ye priests, is it in the prophets or in the Gospel, in the Epistles of St. Paul or the Rules of St. Benedict and St. Augustine, that you find these disputes, these lawsuits, these intrigues for transitory and perishable things?”

— Anthony of Padua, sermon on Sts. Peter and Paul, in C. M. Antony’s English (1911)

He could say such things to a bishop’s face. At a synod at Bourges, Rigauld was told, he turned to the archbishop with the words “I speak to thee, mitre-bearer!” and rebuked him until the archbishop wept.

A nest in the wound of Christ

The most tender of his surviving passages tells the soul where to live. Like a dove that nests in the cleft of a rock, the soul should hide in the wound in Christ’s side, which leads to His Heart, and build its nest there out of the virtues the world despises.

“Be as the dove who makes her nest in the deepest cleft of the rock. This cleft, in which the soul should hide itself, is the wound in the side of Jesus Christ. … The world despises them as useless, but it is with these that we shall build our nest, deep in the Rock, in the Heart of Jesus.”

— Anthony of Padua, sermon, in C. M. Antony’s English (1911)

The virtues he names are humility, gentleness, poverty, patience and mortification. He had practised them long before he preached them: at the hermitage of Monte Paolo he hid his learning, washed the pots and the friars’ feet, and lived on bread and water. He died at Arcella looking upward, and when the friars asked what he saw, he answered, “I see my Lord.”

Holiness in the field of the world

Anthony did not think holiness belonged only to hermits and monks. In a sermon on the lilies of the field, he gave each its place, and the last and the best place went to ordinary penitents living in the world.

“Hermits flourish in the desert, … monks stand like flowers in the cloister garth, protected from the great heat of the sun, but the penitent lives and thrives and blossoms in the field of the world.”

— Anthony of Padua, sermon for the 15th Sunday after Trinity, in C. M. Antony’s English (1911)

He preached that way to the crowds of Padua in 1231, out in the fields because no church could hold them: enemies were reconciled, prisoners set free, and so many came to confess that the priests of the city could not hear them all.

Where will the sinner hide?

Anthony was gentle and severe at once, and the early Latin Life says his hearers felt love and fear together. He spoke of the judgment of God without softening it.

“Whither will the sinner flee; where will he hide? Flight is impossible; he cannot conceal himself! To appear before God is unbearable terror.”

— Anthony of Padua, second sermon for the 2nd Sunday of Lent, in C. M. Antony’s English (1911)

His 1911 biographer mentions the opinion of a modern critic that this sermon may lie behind the hymn Dies Irae. The early Life says famous preachers trembled under his words and hid their faces behind a hand or a sleeve.

Prayer and the Word

Anthony read Scripture in its four senses: the literal, the allegorical, the moral and the anagogical. He taught four attitudes of prayer, which he named in Latin obsecratio, oratio, postulatio and gratiarum actio. In his general audience on Anthony in 2010, Pope Benedict XVI drew out other lines from the sermons: that charity is the soul of faith; that Christ hangs on the cross before us so that we may look at it as into a mirror; and that preaching Jesus softens hard hearts. Those lines are given here in paraphrase, because the modern translations are under copyright. Anthony himself did what he taught: he preached every day of the Lent of 1231, and he spent that winter, though sick, writing his sermons down for other preachers.

quotes.text: But the garment dyed with the blood of the poor shall be the prey of eternal flames.
quotes.source: Anthony, Lenten sermon (Latin checked in Paris 1521 ed., fol. 85). C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), p. 82. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: The usurer … is worse than Judas. That traitor, having sold the Blood of his Divine Master, brought back to the priests and princes the thirty pieces he had received, but the usurer guards and keeps his unjust gains.
quotes.source: Anthony, sermon (locator not given). C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), p. 82. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: Thus when the bucket of almsgiving is let down into the well of riches it makes their possession purer to the conscience and more agreeable to God.
quotes.source: Anthony, sermon. C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), p. 82. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: The devil spreads his web like a spider! The spider begins from the outside and gradually works inwards with thousands of threads, sitting to watch in the centre.
quotes.source: Anthony, sermon for Septuagesima. C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), p. 78. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: So point out by your good example the way of Truth to those that know it not, help on those who are slow, soothe those who are too hasty … bear one another’s burdens.
quotes.source: Anthony, sermon for the 4th Sunday after Trinity (the cranes). C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), p. 79. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: Be as the dove who makes her nest in the deepest cleft of the rock. This cleft, in which the soul should hide itself, is the wound in the side of Jesus Christ.
quotes.source: Anthony, sermon. C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), pp. 79–80. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: The world despises them as useless, but it is with these that we shall build our nest, deep in the Rock, in the Heart of Jesus.
quotes.source: Anthony, sermon (on humility, gentleness, poverty, patience, mortification). C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), p. 80. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: Hermits flourish in the desert, … monks stand like flowers in the cloister garth, protected from the great heat of the sun, but the penitent lives and thrives and blossoms in the field of the world.
quotes.source: Anthony, sermon for the 15th Sunday after Trinity. C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), pp. 78–79. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: Tell me, ye priests, is it in the prophets or in the Gospel, in the Epistles of St. Paul or the Rules of St. Benedict and St. Augustine, that you find these disputes, these lawsuits, these intrigues for transitory and perishable things?
quotes.source: Anthony, sermon on Sts. Peter and Paul. C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), p. 83. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: Whither will the sinner flee; where will he hide? Flight is impossible; he cannot conceal himself! To appear before God is unbearable terror.
quotes.source: Anthony, second sermon for the 2nd Sunday of Lent. C. M. Antony (Woodcock), Saint Antony of Padua, the Miracle Worker (1911), p. 84. https://archive.org/details/StAntonyMiracleWorker

quotes.text: I will take their habit, and so will I, too, go to the fight.

gaps: Biography: about 7,550 words of prose by the lint count (narrative plus the source note and research paragraph; about 8,000 with the 12 block quotes), a little below the tier A range of 8,000–10,000. Reaching the range honestly needs the Assidua, the Liber miraculorum and Peckham's Life.

Not read: the Latin Assidua (and Gamboso's English), the Benignitas, the Dialogus, Peckham's Life, the Raymundina, the Liber miraculorum in full, the Fioretti, the bull Cum dicat Dominus, the list of the 45 canonization miracles.

Not confirmed, left out: Exulta Lusitania felix (text not read; the 1946 Doctorate itself comes from Benedict XVI's audience), the date 16 January 1946, John Paul II's authorization of the 1981 examination (the biography says 'a commission appointed by the Holy See'), the basilica's building dates, the 2015 minor-basilica status, patronages from the Wikipedia summary (Portugal, pregnancy, animals, the sick).

The responsory 'Si quaeris miracula' and the invocation 'The sea obeys, and fetters break': Catholic Encyclopedia gives Julian of Speyer, Coleridge gives Bonaventure, EWTN gives Julian; no Latin text read. Not included as a prayer.
The 'Tony, Tony, turn around' rhyme is not his; origin unknown.

Latin: only the vine passage (in substance; Woodcock's 'Man's soul is a vine' not found word for word) and the purple passage (Woodcock's locator Fer. 6 Dom. I vs Latin found under Feria V of the 2nd week; 'larceny' not in the Latin) were checked. All other sermon quotations are Woodcock's English without a Latin check; the Sunday sermons' Latin was not found online.
Benedict XVI's lines (charity the soul of faith; the cross as a mirror; preaching Jesus melts hard hearts) are paraphrased only: Holy See translation, copyright.

Anthony's words before the anointing are in the early Latin Life (Acta Sanctorum, p. 202) as well as in Rigauld; the English is Woodcock's. The letter of Francis to Anthony first appears in the Liber miraculorum (about 1367); its authenticity is disputed and its wording differs in three sources.
No source read says Anthony met Francis in person; no meeting is narrated.

Date conflicts: tongue found 8 April 1263 (Basilica) or 18 February (CNA); 1350 translation 14 or 15 February; Cardinal Guy de Boulogne or Guy of Montfort; Ezzelino's defeat dated 1259 only by inference; Gregory IX hearing Anthony in Rome in 1227 (Baring-Gould, Butler) or 1230 (Woodcock).
birth_year left null: 1195 is the Bollandists' computation from his age at death (36). Parents' names come from 17th-century writers (Pacheco) and Butler; left out.
Authorship unverified: the Concordantiae morales (Neale 1856) and the Sermones in psalmos (Bologna 1757); not quoted.
Miracle entries for the Basilica's later stories (speaking infant, violent husband, the stabbed wife, Aleardino's glass, the dead man of Lisbon, Eurilia) rest on titles and openings only.

Prayers: none verified. 'O gloriosa Domina' (the hymn he sang at death) is not his and its text is not in the notes. St. Anthony's Bread, the Tuesday devotions and the 'Miraculous Responsory' were not researched.
No image chosen; all candidates unverified.

Checked 2026-10-01 against the raw texts: the canonization dream belongs to a doubting cardinal in the Latin Life, Rigauld and the 1883 chronicle (not the Pope); the war-horse image is Rigauld's only (the Latin Life has the elephant); 'Patarines' is not in the early Lives; the Vercelli appearance is not in the early Lives; the stolen book is a glossed psalter in the 1367 Liber miraculorum and a manuscript of notes in Coleridge and Woodcock, and the figure on the bridge is a devil with an axe in the Liber and a man with a sword in Coleridge.
